articles.title: Don’t Get Me Started: High Cost of a Lopsided Bench
articles.content:
by Dennis Crouch
At the Federal Circuit, the more the judges talk during a party's argument, the less likely that party is to win.
I've been developing a system that does oral argument transcription and then uses voice-matching for speaker identification: https://scotusgate.com/dockets/cafc_arguments.php.
I used those transcripts and timestamps for about 7,000 appeals from the past 20 years -- comparing the relative wordcounts. The chart below shows the trend by sorting the oral arguments into five equal groups -- from those where the judges spoke the least during the appellant’s argument relative to the appellee’s argument (left side of the chart) to those where they spoke the most (right side of the chart).
The gray bars show the appellant’s win rate in each group, falling from 48% to 7%, and the black bars show the same drop (65% to 17%) with Rule 36 affirmances removed (appellants always lose on R.36).
An appellant “won” if the Federal Circuit reversed, vacated, or modified any part of the judgment below. An affirmance counts as a loss. Dismissals and other dispositions (most often settlements) are left out of the analysis.
And one caveat - my study found a hot bench overall is actually good news for appellants -- they won about 46% of the time before the busiest third of panels, compared with about 12% before the quietest third. What this study does is look at when the judicial questioning is lopsided.
I also wanted to test the pattern going forward. During the week of November 2, 2026, the court heard 35 arguments that I was able to rank by the same measure. The chart at the end of this post orders them from the appellant most likely to win (Enovsys v. Uber) to the least likely (Finjan v. Palo Alto Networks). Based upon the study's numbers, I expect about eight appellant wins. As of this morning, five of the 35 have already been decided in Rule 36 affirmances. And another caveat here - I generally am awful at predictions. A recent case in point was this past Tuesday evening (voting day). I arrived home after a dinner with colleagues and told my wife that I really don't think that Democrats will win the Senate...

articles.title: The Wait for Oral Argument at the Federal Circuit
articles.content:
by Dennis Crouch
Parties are now waiting about 19 months from docketing to oral arguments at the Federal Circuit. That is well above the 11 month average in 2021. Decisions still typically follow relatively quickly after arguments, although that time is extended a bit as the court issues fewer R36 judgments without opinion. My data show the wait peaked at about 20 months in 2025 and fallen a bit over the past two years.
What I'm finding here is that the added time is the court's delay after briefing until a slot is given on the argument calendar. This means that a fully briefed appeal waits for about one year for its argument - whereas that was only about four months back in 2021.
In my recent post on visiting judges, I noted that the court has brought back judges sitting by designation after more than five years without one on a merits panel. This wait for argument shows why they are needed.

articles.title: Visiting Judges Return to the Federal Circuit
articles.content:
by Dennis Crouch
Visiting judges are back at the Federal Circuit. So far in 2026, about 17% of the court's merits decisions (opinions and Rule 36 judgments) have come from a panel that included a judge from another court sitting by designation. Before 2024, the court had gone more than five years without a visitor on any merits panel.
Federal Circuit uses visiting judges to help alleviate "heavy caseloads or unanticipated personnel needs." Recall that Judge Newman has been barred from hearing cases since March 2023, so only 11 of the court's 12 active judges have been sitting. And, the court's senior judges handling a smaller share of decisions than they did a few years ago. Meanwhile, the wait-time from docketing to decision has nearly doubled, from about 11 months in 2021 to over 21 months in 2026.

articles.title: Self Citations in the Federal Judiciary
articles.content:
In the paper, we take a deep dive into decisions by the Federal Circuit and Eighth Circuit, looking at the extent to which judges cite their own prior decisions relative to citing those by other judges on the court. We also look at the rate that judges cite their own prior decisions relative to the rate at which they’re cited by other judges. Previous studies have used the rate at which judges cite their own opinion to draw conclusions about their individual behaviors relative to other judges, but to our knowledge no one has previously looked at this topic more broadly.
Our principal finding is that judges disproportionately cite to opinions they authored, but we were surprised by the extent of disproportionate self-citation. At the Federal Circuit, ten of the twelve studied judges cite themselves more than they cite any other judge, as do eleven of the twelve studied judges at the Eighth Circuit. For each judge, we compared self-citations to the number of citations to the third-party judge whom that judge cited most frequently, and the mean differences are a factor of 1.6 and 1.8, respectively. In addition, at both courts, every judge cites themselves more frequently than any other judge cites them. The mean differences are 1.7 and 2, respectively. The following graphs illustrate this for the set of Federal Circuit judges in our study.
The paper also develops a framework for thinking about why judges cite themselves. Dennis mentioned familiarity, which is a likely reason in many instances. But there may be motivations beyond that, including preferred language, doctrinal preference, marketing, and a desire to be consistent with one’s own past decisions. We also consider alternate explanations such clerk behavior and case selection effects, but conclude that they do not significantly explain the results.
If you’re interested in digging into this topic further, a draft of the paper is available on Iowa Research Online. Since the paper is still in draft state, we haven’t published the dataset yet, but are happy to provide it on request if you’re interested in replicating or looking more closely at our analysis.
articles.summary:
By Jason Rantanen and Jason Reinecke
Earlier this week, Dennis posted about the idea of self-citations by judges – that is, judges citing their own work – drawing on a  set of a Federal Circuit cases from 2021-2025 to show that this appears to be the case at the Federal Circuit.
Unbeknownst to him, we’ve been working on a full-legnth study of the extent to which judges engage in the practice of self-citations, a draft of which we’ve just posted to LawArchive.

In the paper, we take a deep dive into decisions by the Federal Circuit and Eighth Circuit, looking at the extent to which judges cite their own prior decisions relative to citing those by other judges on the court. We also look at the rate that judges cite their own prior decisions relative to the rate at which they’re cited by other judges. Previous studies have used the rate at which judges cite their own opinion to draw conclusions about their individual behaviors relative to other judges, but to our knowledge no one has previously looked at this topic more broadly.

Our principal finding is that judges disproportionately cite to opinions they authored, but we were surprised by the extent of disproportionate self-citation. At the Federal Circuit, ten of the twelve studied judges cite themselves more than they cite any other judge, as do eleven of the twelve studied judges at the Eighth Circuit. For each judge, we compared self-citations to the number of citations to the third-party judge whom that judge cited most frequently, and the mean differences are a factor of 1.6 and 1.8, respectively. In addition, at both courts, every judge cites themselves more frequently than any other judge cites them. The mean differences are 1.7 and 2, respectively. The following graphs illustrate this for the set of Federal Circuit judges in our study.

The paper also develops a framework for thinking about why judges cite themselves.  Dennis mentioned familiarity, which is a likely reason in many instances. But there may be motivations beyond that, including preferred language, doctrinal preference, marketing, and a desire to be consistent with one’s own past decisions. We also consider alternate explanations such clerk behavior and case selection effects, but conclude that they do not significantly explain the results.

If you’re interested in digging into this topic further, a draft of the paper is available on Iowa Research Online. Since the paper is still in draft state, we haven’t published the dataset yet, but are happy to provide it on request if you’re interested in replicating or looking more closely at our analysis.
